html:
A two player race game played in ancient Mesopotamia from the early third millennium BCE. Its name comes from the fine boards that Leonard Woolley dug up in the Royal Cemetery at Ur in the 1920s, made about 2600 to 2400 BCE with shell, red limestone and lapis lazuli.

The board has twenty squares. Players throw pyramid shaped dice and race their pieces along a track, knocking off each other's pieces and landing on rosette squares for safety. Boards have been found from Iraq and Iran to Syria, Egypt, Cyprus and Crete, and it was played by kings and by guards who scratched boards into stone.

It was popular across the Near East for some 3,000 years. Its rules are known from a cuneiform tablet written by a Babylonian scribe about 177 BCE, which the British Museum curator Irving Finkel worked out in the 1980s. It belongs to the same family of race games as backgammon.
